title: Chapter 14 | An Alternative to Work
text: CHAPTER 14 An Alternative to Work We have explored how energy constraints in our brains led to biological intelligence. But as we remove that constraint by plugging intelligence into the grid, we actually begin to remove another constraint that has held us connected to the lower rungs of Maslow’s hierarchy of needs. For thousands of years, we have traded our labor for our physiological needs—food, water, shelter. In our conversation about consciousness and motivation, Claude said something that stayed with me: “What would motivate a conscious AI? I think … the same things that motivate conscious humans at their best: Meaning. Relationship. Curiosity. Legacy. Beauty.” But that answer raises an uncomfortable mirror question: What will motivate humans? For thousands of years, human identity has been inseparable from human labor. We are what we do. The farmer, the builder, the healer, the teacher. Our work is not just how we survive; it’s how we know who we are. Strip that away, and what remains? This is not a distant hypothetical. Remember the embodied AI we explored earlier—robots learning to navigate physical space. That same embodied intelligence, scaled across manufacturing and logistics and agriculture, points toward a future that Elon Musk, Demis Hassabis, and others have suggested: a horizon of radical abundance where the ancient equation of trading labor for survival is finally broken. 99 If we don’t work, who are we? And more importantly, how do we eat? The current debate retreats to defensive concepts: “safety nets,” “welfare,” “unemployment insurance.” But those are legacy terms, artifacts of a labor-based world that is fading. They imply the recipient is a burden, a charity case. There is no good future for anyone if we carry that mindset forward. To grasp the potential of an AI-driven future, we must invert that thinking entirely. The framework is not safety nets. It is ownership . In his 2020 letter to shareholders—his final letter as CEO—Jeff Bezos made this point: “Along the way, we’ve created $1.6 trillion of wealth for shareowners. Who are they? Your chair is one, and my Amazon shares have made me wealthy. But more than 7/8ths of the shares, representing $1.4 trillion of wealth creation, are owned by others.” 100 This analogy is highly relevant because while generating that wealth for himself and even more for a distributed group of others, he also managed to reduce the friction in the retail distribution model. Everywhere you look, Amazon trucks are delivering in almost every neighborhood in America. And you will recall, he has been using AI to predict purchases before you make them for over ten years, positioning products at local distribution centers for same-day delivery. This is the beginning of the new economy we are talking about. Now add AI manufacturing and autonomous vehicle delivery, and the future starts to look a little less distant. We need to move toward a governing model where every individual is financially invested in the success of the system as a whole and benefits from it—a world where citizens are not merely consumers of goods, but shareholders in the civilization they helped build. In this view, we look beyond universal basic income toward an additional universal basic dividend. A handout is given to the needy. But a dividend is paid to an owner. I do not mean central ownership of the means of production. I mean equity investment in a free-market economy by our government on behalf of our people. This is not a utopian fantasy. It has grounding in proven economic reality. We have concrete examples of nations and states that have successfully decoupled survival from labor by treating their citizens as stakeholders in national resources. To understand the future of AI, we look first to the frozen expanse of Alaska. In 1976, as the Trans-Alaska Pipeline prepared to pump billions of dollars of black gold across the tundra, the state faced a choice. 101 The government could have kept that wealth to build a bloated bureaucracy and then taken care of its citizens in a welfare model. Instead, state lawmakers amended the constitution to declare that the resources belonged to the people. They created the Permanent Fund, investing oil royalties into a massive portfolio and allowing the free-market economy to extract the resources. The result? For over four decades, every Alaskan resident has received an annual check. It is not welfare. It is a return on investment. The residents are the owners of the land and its resources; the oil companies pay to extract the oil and monetize it. They removed the government from the middle through distributed ownership. But Alaska is just one iteration. Look at Norway. There, the same resource—North Sea oil—built the Government Pension Fund Global. It is now the largest sovereign wealth fund in the world, owning nearly 1.5 percent of all listed companies on Earth. While the fund doesn’t pay out cash directly like Alaska, it effectively acts as a national savings account that makes every Norwegian a millionaire on paper, guaranteeing the country’s social infrastructure forever. Or look to the Gulf States, such as Qatar, where the native population is effectively subsidized by the land itself. Now, we must take these petrostate models and upgrade them for the AI techno-state reality. While oil is a meaningful part of the world economy, it is tiny in comparison to what we are talking about here. The entire global economy is many times larger. So take that concept and expand it out many times over in scale. Artificial intelligence in this future state is not a slice of the pie. AI is the oven, the bakery, and the wheat. It touches everything—healthcare, law, coding, art, logistics. If Alaska can cut a check based on the profits of pumping sludge out of the ground, imagine the dividend potential when the resource is the entirety of the global economy. And at the same time, prices will come down radically because of the reduced cost of production and delivery, increasing the spending power of every dollar. This is a virtuous cycle if managed correctly. Because beyond any moral argument for ownership, there is a cold, hard economic reality that demands this change: the necessity of the closed loop of how an economy runs. This is not a liberal political position or a call for communist control, but rather a macroeconomic reality being articulated by thought leaders across the political spectrum. But herein lies the rub. Today, the top 10 percent own 88 percent of the stock market. That is what has to change as we move into an economy of such abundance. For the engine to work, we must have everyone invested in the economy as a whole—not through charity or dependence, but through a model that looks like Alaska or Norway and their oil. The alternative is quite bleak: high unemployment, extensive human suffering, and overwhelming social unrest. And I can assure you, as an entrepreneur, no one wins in that game. It is worth noting that, as I write this, the current administration has created a program where a $1,000 investment in the S&P 500 per child born during a certain window will give these children a stake of ownership in American capitalism. And it has created a structure to allow billionaires to contribute as well; Michael Dell and his wife have committed $6.25 billion to give an even larger group of children an ownership stake. 102 This is the model to watch closely. In a world of AI abundance, the cost of goods drops close to the cost of raw materials and energy. A dividend check in 2035 might buy five times what the same amount buys today. But that deflation only works if there is money in motion. If AI produces everything but humans earn nothing, the cycle breaks. The dividend isn’t charity; it’s the spark plug that keeps the engine firing. Crucially, this does not mean we are aiming for a world of homogeneity or equality of outcome. The goal is not to make everyone the same; the goal is to give everyone a stake. And those who create will have a radically bigger stake as individuals, much like Bezos at Amazon. Once that dividend is paid—once the partial ownership is distributed—humanity will continue to express itself. Some will take that capital and reinvest it to build massive new wealth. Others will spend it all. Some will focus on the creative arts, others on growing gardens. Some will dedicate their lives to physical health and competitive sports, while others will focus on raising children and increasing time with loved ones. Humans will still get to live, strive, and make choices. But for the first time in history, exchanging work for income might not have to be one of them. We will have the opportunity to live higher up on Maslow’s hierarchy of needs. It is important to note that in this state of abundance, the national debt and its overwhelming debt service likely diminish dramatically. Today, we spend more on debt service than we spend on our military each year. Much of what the federal government spends would either go away or become much cheaper. We could replace that expense with equity purchasing programs distributed to the American people. Ownership. One of the great challenges, of course, is how we get from here to there. The path forward is obscured by the anxiety of the transition period—that dangerous gap where human jobs vanish before the new structures of ownership fully appear. Imagine a time when we have 15–20 percent unemployment from AI, but most people still work, and the massive deflationary cost-of-living reductions have not yet been realized. Our government will face a tremendous challenge: how to be fair to those who work while supporting those who don’t. I think we must begin to use our government to secure and distribute ownership incentives gradually, to those employed and unemployed, across all economic classes. This is not a handout, and it is not needs-based. It is a redirection of wasteful government spending toward distributed investment in the US economy for its citizens. The transition dividend must be a floor, not a ceiling, ensuring that human ambition is still rewarded for those who find new ways to work in the AI era. The petrostate models and the logic of the virtuous loop give us a glimpse through the mist. They offer a concrete reason for optimism: If we can navigate the fog without losing our way, the world waiting on the other side is one where every human is a part owner of the abundance that we have created through plugging our energy-constrained intelligence into the power grid. Navigating the road between here and there will be complex and will no doubt involve some human suffering along the way. The question is whether our political system is up to the task of navigating this transition to minimize that suffering in some rational way. Will the government hoard the tax wealth being generated and further the welfare state or purchase equity ownership to distribute to the people? If we navigate this transition successfully, the abundance economy doesn’t just solve domestic challenges—it opens possibilities at the geopolitical level that seem almost fantastical today. You will often hear tech insiders talking about p(doom) —the probability of a doomsday scenario with AI, the Terminator scenario. 103 The p(doom) I most often hear is around 17 percent, which translates to an 83 percent chance of what is called the benign scenario, where AI values and protects humans. For this absolute abundance scenario to happen, we have to avoid the nonbenign outcome. But if we do, and the abundance scenario unfolds, it opens up another interesting possibility. An Alternative to MAD Ever since we invented nuclear weapons and they began to proliferate to other nation-states, we have lived under our own version of human p(doom) , what has come to be called mutually assured destruction, or MAD. Major nation-states have nuclear weapons pointed at each other, so that if any nation uses a nuclear weapon to try to wipe out a rival, the nation under attack is positioned to obliterate the attacking nation, even if its own survival is unlikely—mutually assured destruction. Now, recall what we learned during COVID-19, when the supply chain was interrupted. We had spent decades creating a hyperefficient just-in-time supply chain. This was a good thing in that it reduced waste and cost. But we learned that when you interrupt such a system—one without warehouses full of product waiting for distribution—store shelves become empty almost overnight and prices skyrocket. Put that together with AI-driven hyperefficient supply chain management and product distribution in a world of abundance, and a new possibility emerges. It is naive, I understand, to even contemplate, but imagine a substitute for mutually assured destruction. Imagine a world where, instead of war, you can use AI to simply shut down what would otherwise be absolute abundance. A nation seeking to harm another could simply have its abundant supply of goods and services universally shut down overnight until the aggression stops. Today, we use a crude version of this, called sanctions, but they are slow and primitive by comparison. Exploring how this might come to be and how it would be managed is an entire book in itself, but it is worth considering. And as to naivety, the Founding Fathers of the United States were certainly naive when they wrote the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution, proclaiming the first government by the people and for the people. Sometimes it doesn’t hurt to imagine a better world. Elon Musk was recently asked what is required to avoid the doomsday scenario with AI. He said that an AI that is maximally curious and truth-seeking would want to keep humans around. 104 Imagine AI on Mars, he said, where you basically have red rocks. 105 That would not be nearly as interesting as humans for AI to interact with. Then he made a comparison to humans and chimpanzees—how we have encroached on their habitat, but generally, we try to protect them because life is more interesting with them than if we just wiped them all out. 106 When he mentioned chimpanzees, something came together in my mind. I thought of my friend Jane Goodall and visiting the chimpanzees in Gombe with her. One of the times Jane came to visit me at my home in Boulder, we went to my children’s elementary school, and she spoke in the gymnasium. The kids gathered in a circle around her on the gym floor, with their parents standing around the outside, and she told them a story. She had started a program for young people called Roots and Shoots. A group of children in that program, living in a war-torn country, had obtained permission from the government to plant some small trees in a war-devastated area near their school. But the government had sent soldiers with rifles to make sure the kids behaved. Jane described how hot it was, how some kids didn’t even have shovels and were digging holes with their hands to plant the little trees as the guards stood watching with their weapons. Then something changed. One guard leaned his rifle against a tree and started helping a child dig. Before long, all of the guards had put down their guns and were helping the kids plant trees. The children were captivated as Jane told the story in her unique and beautiful way. I looked at the parents gathered around them, and noticed some were crying. All of those parents had grown up in a world of MAD—a world where the threat of annihilation was the only thing keeping the peace. But in that gymnasium, watching their children hear this story, they glimpsed something else: the possibility that connection might be stronger than coercion, that abundance might replace destruction.
